1.word_for_word: catvāriṃśe — in the fortieth chapter; akrūraḥ kṛṣṇam īśvara-īśvaram matvā — Akrūra, understanding Kṛṣṇa to be the Lord of lords; praṇamya bhaktyā tuṣṭāva — bowed and praised him with devotion; sa-guṇa-aguṇa-bhedataḥ — in both qualified and transcendent aspects; tvām nataḥ asmi — I bow to you; ādyam puruṣam — the primordial Person; avyayam — imperishable; anādi-nidhanam — without beginning or end; akhila-hetūnām hetum — cause of all causes; nārāyaṇam tvām — you are Nārāyaṇa; yat nābhi-jātāt — from the one born from whose navel; brahmaṇaḥ — Brahmā
1.translation: In the fortieth chapter Akrūra, recognizing Kṛṣṇa as the Lord of lords, bows and praises him devotionally in both his manifest, qualified aspect and his transcendent aspect. ‘O Kṛṣṇa, I bow to you.’ Why should Kṛṣṇa, his younger kinsman, receive such obeisance? Because he is the primordial, imperishable Person, without beginning or end, the cause even of all other causes. If one says, ‘That description belongs to Nārāyaṇa, not to me,’ Akrūra explicitly answers, ‘You are Nārāyaṇa.’ This is not exaggerated praise: Brahmā himself arose from the lotus born from his navel.

2.word_for_word: akhila-hetu-hetutvam prapañcayati — he elaborates being the cause of all causes; khasya ādiḥ ahaṃkāraḥ — ego is the source of ether and the other elements; ajā — unborn Prakṛti, māyā; tasyā ādiḥ puruṣaḥ — the Puruṣa is her source; jagataḥ hetavaḥ — causes of the universe; te sarve tava aṅga-bhūtāḥ — all are limbs or subordinate aspects of you; śrī-mūrteḥ bhūtāḥ — arisen from your divine form; upasarjana-bhūtāḥ vā — or existing as subordinate factors
2.translation: Akrūra elaborates how Kṛṣṇa is the cause of all causes. Ahaṃkāra is the source of ether and the other elements; the unborn Prakṛti or māyā stands behind it; and the Puruṣa is the source of that Prakṛti. All these causes of the universe are nevertheless limbs or subordinate manifestations of Kṛṣṇa, arising from or dependent upon his divine form.

3.word_for_word: ati-stutiḥ katham — why such excessive praise?; aham eva anyataḥ utpannaḥ tat-paratantraḥ ca — I myself am produced from another and dependent; tava eṣā māyā — this is your māyā; tvat-pāramārthyam na kaḥ api veda — no one knows your ultimate reality; ete ajā-ādayaḥ — these beginning with the unborn Prakṛti; ātmanaḥ te svarūpam na viduḥ — do not know your own nature; anātmatayā jaḍatvena — because they are insentient, not the conscious Self; gṛhītāḥ pratyakṣa-ādibhiḥ dṛṣṭāḥ — apprehended as objects by perception and other means; ajaḥ brahmā api ajāyā guṇaiḥ anubaddhaḥ — even unborn Brahmā is bound by the guṇas of Prakṛti; guṇātītam te svarūpam na veda — he does not know your nature beyond the guṇas; jīvaḥ tān ātmānam ca vetti — the jīva knows those principles and itself; na punaḥ tvat-svarūpam — but not your true nature
3.translation: A doubt arises: is this not excessive praise, since Kṛṣṇa appears to have taken birth from others and to be dependent upon them? Akrūra answers that such appearance belongs to Kṛṣṇa's māyā; no one thereby knows his ultimate reality. Prakṛti and the other causal principles cannot know his nature because they are insentient objects, themselves apprehended through perception and other means of knowledge. Even Brahmā, though called unborn, is enveloped by the guṇas of Prakṛti and therefore does not know Kṛṣṇa's nature beyond the guṇas; how then could others? Alternatively, Prakṛti and the other insentient principles know neither themselves nor Kṛṣṇa, whereas the conscious jīva can know those principles and itself but still cannot know Kṛṣṇa's limitless nature. The cited verse of the Haṃsa-guhya makes this same distinction.

4.word_for_word: yadi ke api na jānanti katham saṃsāra-nivṛttiḥ — if no one knows him directly, how can beings escape saṃsāra?; sākṣāt agocaratve api — although not directly an object of cognition; yena kena api mārgeṇa bhajatām — for those worshiping through one or another path; tvam gamyaḥ asi — you are attainable; hairaṇya-garbha-ādayaḥ — followers of the Hiraṇyagarbha path and others; adhyātma-adhibhūta-adhidaiva-sākṣiṇam — witness of the individual, material and divine levels; mahā-puruṣam — the Great Person; antar-yāmi-svarūpam — in the form of the indwelling ruler; īśvaram niyantāram — Lord and controller; yajanti — worship
4.translation: If Kṛṣṇa cannot be directly comprehended, how can living beings escape saṃsāra? Although he is not available as an ordinary object of direct cognition, he becomes attainable to those who worship him by the various valid paths. Those who follow the Hiraṇyagarbha and yogic paths worship the Great Person as witness of the adhyātma, adhibhūta and adhidaiva levels and as the indwelling Lord who controls them.

5.word_for_word: sāṅkhya-yogau ekī-kṛtya uktau — Sāṅkhya and Yoga have been stated together; trayī-mārgam karma-jñāna-bhedena darśayati — he now shows the Vedic path divided into ritual action and knowledge; vaitānikāḥ karma-yoginaḥ — performers of Vedic sacrificial rites; tvām eva yajante — worship you alone; indra-varuṇa-vāyu-ādīn yajante — they appear to worship Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu and others; nānā vajra-hasta-ādīni rūpāṇi yeṣām — whose forms bear different names such as the wielder of the thunderbolt; teṣām amarāṇām ākhyayā — under the names of those gods; tvām eva yajanti — they worship you alone; sarveśvarāḥ bahavaḥ na sambhavanti — there cannot be many independent supreme Lords; nāma-bhedena — by difference of name
5.translation: Having treated Sāṅkhya and Yoga together, Akrūra next presents the Vedic path in its ritual and contemplative forms. The Vedic sacrificers worship Kṛṣṇa himself. Although their rites are addressed to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu and other gods under differing names and forms such as ‘the wielder of the thunderbolt,’ the hymns attribute sovereign powers to those deities; since there cannot be many independent Supreme Lords, such worship ultimately reaches the one Lord through differing divine names. Śrīdhara cites a Vedic passage to support this understanding.

6.word_for_word: jñāna-yajñena — by the sacrifice of knowledge; samādhinā — through contemplative absorption
6.translation: ‘By the sacrifice of knowledge’ means through samādhi, contemplative absorption.

7.word_for_word: sāṅkhya-yoga-trayī-mārgāḥ uktāḥ — Sāṅkhya, Yoga and the Vedic path have been described; vaiṣṇava-śaiva-mārgau — now the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva paths; saṃskṛta-ātmānaḥ — ritually consecrated; vaiṣṇava-śaiva-dīkṣayā dīkṣitāḥ — initiated by Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva dīkṣā; tvayā abhihitena pañcarātra-ādi-vidhinā — by the procedure taught by you, such as Pañcarātra; tvat-mayāḥ — regarding themselves as pervaded by you; tvad-eka-pradhānāḥ — having you alone as their chief object; vāsudeva-saṅkarṣaṇa-pradyumna-aniruddha-bhedena bahu-mūrtim — manifested in the fourfold forms Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha; nārāyaṇa-rūpeṇa eka-mūrtikam — also one form as Nārāyaṇa; tvām eva yajanti — worship you alone
7.translation: After Sāṅkhya, Yoga and the Vedic path, Akrūra speaks of the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva approaches. Those consecrated through such initiations worship according to procedures taught by the Lord, such as Pañcarātra. ‘Tvat-maya’ may mean that they contemplate themselves as pervaded by him, or that he alone is their principal object of worship. They worship the one Lord in the multiple forms of Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha and also in the single form of Nārāyaṇa.

8.word_for_word: bahu-ācārya-vibhedena — through distinctions among many teachers; nānā-bheda-śaiva-pāśupata-ādi-mārgeṇa — by the various Śaiva, Pāśupata and related paths
8.translation: The plurality described here arises from differences among teachers and from the various Śaiva, Pāśupata and related systems.

9.word_for_word: kṣudra-devatā-bhaktāḥ api — even worshipers of lesser deities; tvām eva yajanti — ultimately worship you; he sarva-deva-maya — O one who contains all the gods; paraspara-devatā-adhikṣepa-kalaha-vyākula-cittāḥ — their minds disturbed by quarrels that belittle one another's deities; yadyapi anya-dhiyaḥ — although their conceptions differ; buddhi-mātra-bhedaḥ — difference only in conception; na vastu-bhedaḥ — not difference in the underlying reality
9.translation: Even devotees of lesser deities ultimately worship Kṛṣṇa, for he is ‘the one in whom all the gods are contained.’ One may object that such worshipers often quarrel and disparage one another's deities; how then can they all be worshiping the same being? Śrīdhara answers that the difference lies in their conceptions, not in the ultimate reality to which worship is directed.

10.word_for_word: sarve mārgāḥ tvayi eva paryavasyanti — all paths ultimately terminate in you; adreḥ sakāśāt sarvataḥ prabhavanti yāḥ nadyaḥ — rivers arising on every side from a mountain; parjanyena āpūritāḥ — filled by rain; bahu-srotasaḥ — having many channels; sarvataḥ sindhum eva viśanti — enter the ocean from all directions; tadvat etāḥ gatayaḥ mārgāḥ antataḥ tvām eva viśanti — likewise these paths ultimately enter you
10.translation: All these paths ultimately terminate in Kṛṣṇa. The comparison is with rivers arising on every side of a mountain, swollen by rain and flowing through many channels, yet all eventually entering the ocean. In the same way, these different courses ultimately enter the one Lord.

11.word_for_word: bhavataḥ śaktiḥ yā prakṛtiḥ — Prakṛti, which is your power; tasyāḥ sattva-ādayaḥ guṇāḥ — its guṇas beginning with sattva; prākṛtāḥ prakṛti-kāra-upādhayaḥ — natural limiting conditions produced by Prakṛti; brahma-paryantāḥ sthāvara-ādayaḥ jīvāḥ — beings from immovable organisms up to Brahmā; sva-upādhi-dvārā teṣu guṇeṣu protāḥ — woven into those guṇas through their respective limiting conditions; te guṇāḥ prakṛtau — the guṇas are in Prakṛti; sā ca tvayi — and Prakṛti is in you; upādhi-layāt sarve tvām eva viśanti — with dissolution of limiting conditions all enter you; yad vā — alternatively; brahma-ādayaḥ bhavad-vyatiriktāḥ na santi — Brahmā and the rest are not independent of you
11.translation: The reason all paths terminate in him is that Prakṛti itself is his power. Its modes—sattva, rajas and tamas—form the natural limiting conditions of embodied beings, from stationary life all the way to Brahmā. Those beings are woven into the guṇas through their respective bodies and conditions; the guṇas rest in Prakṛti, and Prakṛti rests in Kṛṣṇa. Thus, as those limiting conditions dissolve, all ultimately enter him. Alternatively, the point is that Brahmā and every other being woven into Prakṛti's guṇas have no existence independent of Kṛṣṇa; hence he contains all the gods.

12.word_for_word: mama api prakṛti-sambandham brūṣi — you seem also to connect me with Prakṛti; teṣām mama ca kaḥ viśeṣaḥ — what then distinguishes me from them?; avibhakta-dṛṣṭaye — whose vision is undivided; alipta-buddhaye — whose awareness is unstained; sarvātmane — being the Self of all; sva-vyatirikta-abhāvāt — because nothing exists outside you; sarva-dhiyām sākṣiṇe — witness of all intellects; na kvāpi buddhi-lepaḥ — nowhere stained by an intellect; guṇa-pravāhaḥ — stream of the guṇas; deva-nṛ-tiryak-ātmānaḥ — beings identifying with divine, human and animal bodies; tvad-avidyayā kṛtaḥ — produced by your avidyā potency
12.translation: Akrūra's statement ‘your Prakṛti’ might appear to connect Kṛṣṇa with Prakṛti just as other beings are connected with it. He therefore states the difference. Kṛṣṇa has undivided vision and unstained awareness because he is the Self of all and nothing exists outside him as a separate object. He is the witness of every intellect and therefore is never stained by any intellect. Ordinary beings, by contrast, identify themselves with divine, human, animal and other bodies and are carried along by the stream of guṇas produced through the Lord's avidyā potency. The distinction is therefore fundamental.

13.word_for_word: sa-guṇam stauti — he praises the Lord's cosmic qualified form; agniḥ mukham — fire is his mouth; agni-ādīn anūdya īśvara-avayavatā vidhīyate — fire and the others are identified as limbs of the Lord; īkṣaṇam — sight, eye; śrutiḥ — hearing faculty; kam — sky; mūrdhā — head; prāṇaḥ ca balam ca — life-breath and strength
13.translation: Having called him the Self of all, Akrūra now praises his cosmic form with attributes. Fire and the other cosmic principles are first named and then identified as limbs of the Lord: ‘this fire is your mouth,’ and so forth. ‘Īkṣaṇa’ means the eye or faculty of sight; ‘śruti’ the faculty of hearing; ‘kam’ the sky; and the relevant phrase includes both vital breath and strength.

14.word_for_word: adrayaḥ — mountains; parasya te — of you, the Supreme; asthi-nakhāni — bones and nails
14.translation: The mountains are described as the bones and nails of your supreme cosmic form.

15.word_for_word: sarvaḥ ayam prapañcaḥ tvad-avayava-bhūtaḥ — this entire cosmos is constituted as your limbs; prapañcasya ṣaṭ janma-ādayaḥ vikārāḥ tvayi na prasajjante — the six transformations beginning with birth that belong to the cosmos do not attach to you; tasya tvayi kalpitatvāt — because the cosmos is superimposed upon you; avyaya-ātmani puruṣe pūrṇe — in the complete imperishable Self, the Puruṣa; lokādayaḥ sañjihate pracaranti — the worlds move and circulate; mano-maye — apprehended through the mind, or whose chief expression is through mind; mano-vṛtti-vyaṅgye — manifested to cognition through a mental mode; jale jalaukasaḥ — aquatic beings in water; udumbara-antaḥ-keśareṣu maśakāḥ — tiny insects within a fig; anantāni brahmāṇḍāni tvayi sañcaranti — countless universes move within you
15.translation: The cosmic body is not limited to the items just mentioned: the whole universe may be regarded as his limbs. Yet the six transformations of created things, beginning with birth, do not therefore apply to Kṛṣṇa, because the cosmos is superimposed upon him rather than constituting his essential nature. Countless worlds move within the complete, imperishable Puruṣa. ‘Mano-maya’ indicates that he is apprehended through the refined mind or manifested to cognition through a mental mode, as supported by the Upaniṣadic statements cited by Śrīdhara. Countless universes circulate within him just as aquatic creatures move in water or minute insects live within the interior of a fig without awareness of one another.

16.word_for_word: tava svarūpam duravagāham — your true nature is difficult to penetrate; tvad-avatāra-kathāmṛtam eva santaḥ sevante — therefore the good resort to the nectar of accounts of your descents; āmṛṣṭā parimārjitā śuk yeṣām — whose grief has been wiped and cleansed away
16.translation: Because such a nature of the Lord is exceedingly difficult to fathom, the saints instead relish the nectar of the narratives of his avatāras. Through that nectar their grief is wiped away and thoroughly cleansed.

17.word_for_word: avatārān namasyati — he bows to the avatāras; haya-śīrṣe — to the Horse-headed Lord; hayagrīvāya — Hayagrīva; madhu-kaiṭabhayoḥ mṛtyave — death of Madhu and Kaiṭabha; hantre — slayer
17.translation: Akrūra now bows to the Lord's avatāras. ‘Haya-śīrṣa’ means Hayagrīva, the Horse-headed Lord, the slayer and death of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.

18.word_for_word: akūpārāya — to the great tortoise; kūrmāya — to Kūrma; kṣiti-uddhāraḥ vihāraḥ yasya — whose sport is the raising of the earth
18.translation: ‘Akūpāra’ refers to the great tortoise, Kūrma. The following description refers to the avatāra whose sport is the raising of the earth.

20.word_for_word: bhṛgūṇām pataye — lord or chief among the Bhṛgus; paraśurāmāya — to Paraśurāma
20.translation: ‘Lord of the Bhṛgus’ refers to Paraśurāma.

21.word_for_word: catur-vyūha-rūpeṇa praṇamati — he bows to the Lord in the form of the four vyūhas; namas te vāsudevāya iti — beginning ‘obeisance to Vāsudeva’
21.translation: Akrūra next offers obeisance to the Lord in the fourfold vyūha form, beginning with ‘obeisance to Vāsudeva.’

23.word_for_word: bandha-mokṣam prārthayitum — to pray for release from bondage; asati deha-ādau grāhaḥ āgrahaḥ yasya — one who clings insistently to unreal things such as the body; asan grāhaḥ yasya iti vā — alternatively, one whose grasp itself is false
23.translation: Having completed the praise, Akrūra begins to pray for release from bondage. The expression may describe one who stubbornly grasps unreal things such as the body, or one whose very grasp of them is false and mistaken.

24.word_for_word: na kevalam ayam lokaḥ — not only the world in general; aham api tathā eva — I too am exactly like this; aham ca iti — expressed by ‘and I’
24.translation: He makes the confession personal: not only the world in general is deluded in this manner; ‘I too am exactly the same.’

25.word_for_word: viparyaya-matiḥ — one whose understanding is inverted; anitye karma-phale nityam iti — regarding temporary karmic results as permanent; anātmani dehe ātmā iti — regarding the non-self body as the self; duḥkha-rūpe gṛha-ādau sukham iti — regarding home and other sources of suffering as happiness; dvandveṣu sukha-duḥkha-ādiṣu āramati — plays and delights among dualities such as pleasure and pain; tamo-viṣṭaḥ — engulfed in darkness; ātmanaḥ priyam prema-āspadam tvām na jāne — I do not recognize you, the true beloved of the self
25.translation: ‘Viparyaya-mati’ means having an inverted understanding: regarding temporary karmic fruits as permanent, the body—which is not the Self—as the Self, and the home and other sources of suffering as true happiness. Such a person plays among the dualities of pleasure and pain. How could anyone delight in pain? Because, engulfed in darkness, I fail to recognize you, the true beloved and proper object of the Self's love.

26.word_for_word: sa-dṛṣṭāntam āha — he states it with an analogy; tasmāt jalāt udbhavanti iti tad-udbhavāni tṛṇa-ādīni — grasses and other growths that arise from that water; taiḥ — by them; māyā-channam tvām — you, hidden by māyā; hitvā — abandoning; parāṅ-mukhaḥ — turning away; deha-abhimukhaḥ — facing toward bodily identification
26.translation: He illustrates the condition with an analogy involving grasses and other growths that arise from water yet obscure it. In the same way, I turn away from you, who are hidden by your māyā, and direct myself instead toward identification with the body.

27.word_for_word: evam jānataḥ kutaḥ viṣaya-abhimukhatā — if you know this, why remain turned toward sense objects?; na utsahe — I am unable; kṛpaṇā viṣaya-vāsanā-yuktā dhīḥ yasya — whose wretched mind is filled with latent desire for objects; kāma-karmabhyām hatam kṣubhitam — struck and agitated by desire and karma; indriyaiḥ balibhiḥ viṣaya-saṃyuktaiḥ — by powerful senses joined to their objects; itaḥ tataḥ ākṛṣyamāṇam manaḥ — mind dragged here and there; roddhum niyantum na śaknomi — I cannot restrain or govern it
27.translation: One may ask why, knowing all this, Akrūra remains turned toward sense objects. His answer is: ‘I am unable to master myself. My wretched intelligence remains filled with impressions of sense desire. My mind is agitated by desire and karma and dragged here and there by powerful senses attached to their objects; I cannot restrain or govern it.’

28.word_for_word: asvatantraḥ yaḥ saḥ aham — I, who am not independent; tava aṅghrim upagataḥ — have approached your feet; śaraṇam prāptaḥ — have taken refuge; indriya-paratantrasya etat api kutaḥ — how can even this be possible for one enslaved by his senses?; he īśa antaryāmin — O Lord, indwelling controller; tvad-aṅghri-upagamanam asatām durāpam — approach to your feet is difficult for the unholy; bhavataḥ anugrahaḥ eva — it must therefore be your grace; puṃsaḥ jīvasya saṃsārasya apavargaḥ — the ending of a living being's saṃsāra; yadā tvat-kṛpayā bhavet — when through your grace it becomes possible; tadā sat-upāsanā sampadyate — then service of the holy arises; tayā eva tvayi matiḥ — through that comes awareness directed toward you; tvat-kṛpām vinā na sat-sevā na tvat-matiḥ na muktir — without your grace there is neither service of saints, thought of you, nor liberation
28.translation: Thus, although he lacks independence and is controlled by his senses, Akrūra has come to the Lord's feet and taken refuge. How could even that happen? ‘O Lord, indwelling controller, reaching your feet is difficult for the unholy; therefore I regard this very approach as your grace.’ One might say that association with saints, rather than direct divine grace, brings about such devotion. Śrīdhara answers that even saintly association arises when, through the Lord's grace, the end of a living being's saṃsāra becomes possible. Through service of the good comes thought directed toward Kṛṣṇa. Without his grace there is no service of saints, no mind fixed on him and certainly no liberation.

29.word_for_word: pādayoḥ patan prārthayate — falling at his feet, he prays; vijñānam eva mātrā mūrtiḥ yasya — whose form consists solely of conscious knowledge; sarva-pratyaya-hetave — cause of every cognition; samasta-jñāna-kāraṇāya — source of all knowledge; puruṣasya ye īśāḥ — powers governing the individual; sukha-duḥkha-ādi-prāpakāḥ kāla-karma-svabhāva-ādayaḥ — time, karma, inherent nature and others that bring pleasure and pain; teṣām pradhānāya niyantre — their chief and controller; brahmaṇe paripūrṇāya — the complete Brahman; ananta-śaktaye — possessing endless potencies; yad vā anantā māyā-ākhyā śaktiḥ yasya — or possessing the boundless power called māyā; pradhānam prakṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ tat-pravartakaḥ īśaḥ kālaḥ — Prakṛti, Puruṣa who activates it, and Time; etat tritaya-ātmane — embodying this triad
29.translation: Falling at the Lord's feet, Akrūra prays in two verses. He bows to the one whose form consists solely of consciousness and who is therefore the cause of every cognition and all knowledge; to the controller of the powers that govern embodied beings, such as time, karma and inherent nature, which produce pleasure and pain; to the complete Brahman of endless potencies. ‘Ananta-śakti’ may also mean one who possesses the immeasurable potency called māyā. Another interpretation takes the verse as referring to the triad of Pradhāna or Prakṛti, the Puruṣa who sets it in motion, and Time, all unified in Brahman; Śrīdhara cites the Lord's later statement that he is this triad.

30.word_for_word: sarva-pratyaya-hetutvam abhivyañjayan — further expressing that he is the cause of every cognition; vāsudevāya — to Vāsudeva, presiding deity of citta; citta-adhiṣṭhātre — controller of mind-stuff; sarva-bhūta-kṣayāya — refuge of all beings; kṣayaḥ āśrayaḥ — kṣaya means abode or refuge; ahaṃkāraḥ prāṇinām āśrayaḥ — ahaṃkāra is a support of embodied beings; saṅkarṣaṇāya — to Saṅkarṣaṇa, presiding over ahaṃkāra; hṛṣīkeśa — Hṛṣīkeśa; buddhi-manasoḥ adhiṣṭhātroḥ pradyumna-aniruddhayoḥ ekīkṛtya grahaṇam — jointly referring to Pradyumna and Aniruddha, controllers of intellect and mind; śaraṇāgatam mām pāhi — protect me who has taken refuge
30.translation: The final verse further expresses the Lord as the ground of cognition. Vāsudeva presides over citta. ‘Kṣaya’ means abode or support, and in the fourfold analysis Saṅkarṣaṇa presides over ahaṃkāra, itself a support for embodied identity. ‘Hṛṣīkeśa’ here gathers together Pradyumna and Aniruddha as the presiding deities of intellect and mind. The prayer concludes simply: ‘Protect me, for I have taken refuge in you.’
